title: Paramedics tell inquest they were surprised that Vancouver woman who had stopped breathing wasn't getting CPR
subtitle: Paramedics called to attend to a person not breathing at Vancouver jail arrived to see the woman lying on her back on the pavement with a number of jail and medical staff surrounding but not treating her. article: Paramedics called to attend to a person not breathing at Vancouver jail arrived to see the woman lying on her back on the pavement with a number of jail and medical staff surrounding but not treating her.
"Were you surprised there was no CPR being done when you arrived?" Rodrick MacKenzie, lawyer for the Coroner's Service of B.C., asked paramedic Mike Burgwin.

"Yes," Burgwin told an inquest into the death of Cheryl Ann Cowan, 58, who had been picked up on a drunken break-and-enter/trespassing charge at her estranged husband's Dunbar home on Dec. 15, 2014 and placed in a police transport van.
"I was wondering why we weren't doing it in the first place," he said. "There was still some confusion about whether it should be done, yes or no, and they asked me and I said 'yes.'"

After being in the police van for 48 minutes, Cowan was found slumped in her seat with no pulse, a fixed stare, blue lips and low body temperature. In a video played at the inquest, she was seen being placed in a wheelchair and then on the ground.
Among those present were the on-duty jail doctor, two jail nurses, the jail sergeant, the Vancouver police constable who drove the van and other jail staff, including sheriffs.

Paramedic Katelyn McRae told the inquest: "I felt that CPR should have been initiated (before paramedics arrived) because they're all trained professionals. It's a pretty standard intervention for a cardiac arrest."
It was the second day of the inquest with a five-person jury who may make recommendations to prevent similar deaths but not assess blame for the death.

The jail doctor, Dr. Brendan Russell, testified he remembers telling others: "She's gone." A nurse testified on Monday that she asked the jail sergeant and the doctor if she should start CPR and was told no, despite her inclination to do so.
Cowan was resuscitated by paramedics but remained on life support until she died eight days later, of lack of oxygen to the brain caused by a heart attack.
The inquest will sit again on Wednesday before the jury retires to consider any recommendations.

A number of witnesses testified there appeared to be no obvious line of command at the scene, and Dr. Russell said he would recommend all jail staff be trained in CPR, jails institute a "code blue" or emergency alert protocol, as is used at hospitals, and staff be required to participate in mock training sessions.
He and other witnesses recommended that police transport wagons be equipped with video cameras that could be monitored remotely.
